title: Comprehensive Surface Irrigation Guide: Principles, Design, and Optimization
html:
Introduction to Surface Irrigation

Surface irrigation is one of the oldest and most common irrigation methods in Iran, where water is conveyed to cultivated fields via canals without pressure. This method is still used in many regions of the country due to its simplicity, low installation cost, and lack of need for complex mechanical infrastructure. However, for optimal efficiency and to prevent the waste of valuable water resources, a precise understanding of surface irrigation principles, including flow rate calculation, proper channel design, and avoidance of water loss, is essential. In this section of the guide, we examine the fundamentals of this method so that you can prevent water waste and increase crop yield through proper layout and smart management.

To better understand the relationship between the irrigation system and crop performance, it is also useful to study the factors affecting the performance of various crops. For example, to learn about the factors influencing watermelon yield in surface systems, you can read the article Factors for Increasing Watermelon Yield per Hectare If you are looking for a guide on pumpkin planting and its irrigation methods, Comprehensive Guide to Pumpkin Planting can be a useful resource that explains the interaction of soil and moisture with plant roots.

Principles and Mechanism of Surface Irrigation

The primary mechanism of surface irrigation is based on the movement of water over the soil surface via gravity. This method is mainly classified into 'flood' (Furrow) and 'basin' (Basin) systems. In the flood method, water is introduced into the irrigation furrows from main channels and moves in parallel. The primary objective is to create uniform and homogeneous soil moisture at the root zone. Ignoring the principles of this mechanism results in asymmetric water distribution and reduced performance.

Key design criteria

To design an efficient surface irrigation system, the following criteria must be carefully examined:

  • Longitudinal soil gradient: The appropriate gradient is typically between 1 and 2 percent. Excessive gradient causes accelerated flow and soil erosion, whereas a low gradient leads to water accumulation and waterlogging in the upstream area.
  • Soil type: Water absorption in sandy (coarse) soils is slower, which is more suitable for surface irrigation as it allows for more uniform guidance. In clay soils with low permeability, irrigation timing must be managed with greater precision.
  • Irrigation timing: It must be calculated how long it takes for the water to travel the length of the field to reach the end of the lateral line. This duration must be adjusted so that moisture does not reach the root depth of the plants, preventing deep percolation.

While surface irrigation is a classic method, tip-type drip irrigation is considered a more precise approach that has gained many advocates in recent years. Familiarizing yourself with the features of tip-type drip laterals can expand your perspective on water management. For technical information and details regarding the quality and durability of these laterals, you can refer to the article Ideal wall thickness of tip-type drip irrigation laterals This information will help you make a better choice when combining systems or upgrading infrastructure.

Optimizing water use in surface irrigation

One of the main challenges of surface irrigation is its relatively low efficiency coefficient compared to pressurized methods. To improve efficiency, focus must be placed on three main axes: system calibration, slope management, and precise irrigation timing. Below is a short guide for calculating irrigation requirements:

  1. Soil Moisture Test: Check the moisture level using simplified methods or digital equipment to prevent redundant irrigation.
  2. Calculating Required Flow Rate: Adjust the water inlet flow rate based on the area and soil type. High flow rates are dangerous for clay soils.
  3. Monitoring Zones: Prevent repeated water intrusion into drier patches and direct the flow to ensure uniform coverage.

For crops with deep root systems, such as dill, surface irrigation can lead to optimal water absorption from deep soil layers when timed appropriately. For more information about crops like dill and how to increase it, you can read the article on dill yield per hectare. Understanding the water requirements of each plant is key to adjusting surface irrigation cycles.

Comparison of surface irrigation with tape and drip methods

Comparing methods helps you make the best choice based on weather conditions, soil type, and budget. Each method has its own advantages and disadvantages, and a correct selection can reduce water and energy costs by up to 30 percent.

Feature Surface irrigation Tape irrigation Drip irrigation
Installation cost Low Average Highest
Water use efficiency 50 to 65 percent 85 to 90 percent 90 to 95 percent
Suitable soil type Silty to clay soils Most soils Most soils (Best for saline soils)
Labor requirements Highest Medium Lowest

Practical tips

For better implementation of surface irrigation in farms, it is recommended to observe the following points to prevent common issues:

  • Laser Leveling: Level the land surface before each irrigation to ensure uniform water flow and prevent local pooling.
  • Bund Building: In furrow irrigation systems, construct appropriate earth banks around each section to control the speed of water discharge and ensure uniform irrigation time.
  • Stepped Water Supply: For slopes exceeding 2%, use stepped canals (check dams) to reduce soil erosion and ensure slow water movement.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Is surface irrigation suitable for all crops?

No. This method is more suitable for crops with deeper roots, such as corn, wheat, and barley. For shallow-rooted grain crops, subsurface systems like tape or drip are usually more effective. If your crop is sunflower, you can refer to the article on factors affecting sunflower yield per hectare for more details. Factors affecting sunflower seed yield per hectare to better understand specific water requirements.

What is the primary cause of water loss with this method?

The main reason is excessive water movement due to uncalibrated flow rate or an incorrect field gradient, which leads to deep percolation into the soil profile and prevents plant roots from accessing it. This issue can also cause salinization of the surface layers.

Summary and final recommendations

Although it is an older technique, surface irrigation remains a cost-effective and efficient solution for many farmers when properly designed and implemented. The key to success in this method lies in attention to details such as field gradient, soil type, and inflow rate. By combining surface irrigation with precise optimization principles, you can increase water efficiency while maintaining final yield. Finally, studying broader agricultural resources, including seed quantity calculation and crop requirements, can help you align your irrigation system with your farm conditions.
